name: Queen's Guild
blurb: Deeper tricks, a real opening plan, endgames, and how to think about a whole game.
who: For a player who already spots forks and pins and wants to get properly good.

lessons.name: Say It Out Loud
lessons.big: Checks, captures, threats. Before every move.

steps.text: From here on, one habit matters more than any trick. Before every move, list three things.
Every check you can give. Every capture you can make. Every threat you can create. Then the same for them.

steps.ask: Start with the checks. Tap the two squares where your rook or queen could give check.
steps.hint: The rook can reach one of them. The queen can reach the other.
steps.why: Re8 and Qb8 are both check. Forcing moves first, always — they narrow the game down.

steps.ask: One of those two checks wins. Play it: move your rook up to e8.
steps.hint: Give the rook away on e8. Look at what the queen does afterwards.
steps.wrongSay: The other one. Think about what happens when they take it.

steps.text: They must take. And now the queen comes to the same square.

steps.ask: Bring your queen to e8. That is checkmate and the game is over.
steps.hint: The queen takes on e8, and the king has nowhere to go.
steps.wrongSay: Take on e8 with the queen.

steps.goal: Five mates in two. List the checks first, every time.

steps.text: Checks, captures, threats. Out loud if it helps.

lessons.name: Look Over Here
lessons.big: Drag the guard away from its job.

steps.text: A defender can only be in one place. Give it something it cannot refuse, and its old job goes undone.

steps.cap: The rook on d8 is guarding the back row. The queen behind it is guarding the rook.

steps.ask: Drag the queen away from the rook. Take it.
steps.hint: Your queen can reach d7. Giving her up is the point.
steps.wrongSay: Take the queen on d7, even though it looks mad.

steps.text: They take back, and the rook has left the back row to do it.

steps.ask: The back row is empty now. Play the checkmate: rook to e8.
steps.hint: Nothing guards e8 any more.
steps.wrongSay: The back row. Nothing is watching it now.

steps.goal: Five of them. Find the defender and give it a better offer.

steps.text: Hey, look over here.

lessons.name: Bait on the Hook
lessons.big: Lure a piece onto a bad square.

steps.text: A decoy is the other way round. You do not drag a piece away. You drag it somewhere terrible.

steps.cap: Pull their king to h8. Then your knight forks the king and the queen.

steps.ask: Offer the rook on h8 and pull him there.
steps.hint: He has to take it. That is what makes it work.
steps.wrongSay: h8. Give the rook away on purpose.

steps.text: He takes, because he has no choice. Now he is on the wrong square.

steps.ask: Fork the king and the queen.
steps.hint: A knight on f7 checks him and hits d8 at the same time.
steps.wrongSay: f7. Check him and hit the queen together.

steps.goal: Five decoys. Bait, then the fork.

steps.text: Bait on the hook.

lessons.name: Wait, First This
lessons.big: Before you take back, is there a check?

steps.text: When they take a piece, taking back feels like the only move. Sometimes there is a better one first.

steps.cap: White has just taken on c6. The obvious move is to take the bishop back with the pawn.

steps.text: But the bishop on c6 is not going anywhere. So look for a check first.

steps.ask: Do not take back yet. Give a check first, with your bishop on f2.
steps.hint: Your bishop on c5 can take on f2 with check.
steps.wrongSay: Look for a check, not a recapture. Something takes on f2.

steps.text: They must answer the check. Then you take on c6 anyway, a whole pawn ahead.

steps.ask: What is the question to ask before every recapture?

choices.text: Is there a check or a bigger threat first?
Which piece should take back?

steps.why: The piece that took is usually stuck there for a move. That move is yours.

steps.text: Wait. First this.

lessons.name: The Busy Babysitter
lessons.big: One defender with two jobs cannot do both.

steps.text: Some pieces have two jobs at once. Give it one job to do, and the other one falls apart.

steps.cap: The queen on e7 is guarding the rook on d8 AND the bishop on e5. Two jobs, one piece.

steps.ask: Make her choose. Take the rook.
steps.hint: Your rook takes on d8, with check.
steps.wrongSay: Take the rook on d8 and see what she has to do.

steps.text: She has to take back. And the bishop is now on its own.

steps.ask: Now take the bishop on e5 with your queen. Nothing is guarding it any more.
steps.hint: Your queen looks straight along the diagonal at e5.
steps.wrongSay: The bishop on e5. Nothing is guarding it now.

steps.ask: How do you spot an overloaded piece?

choices.text: Count what each defender is guarding. Two things is a target
It is always the queen

steps.why: Look at their defenders and count their jobs. Anything with two is a way in.

steps.text: One babysitter, two children.
A piece can attack through another one. It cannot take yet, but it is waiting.

steps.ask: Your rook is on d1. What is it really aiming at, further up the column?
steps.hint: Look past the black bishop on d5, all the way up.
steps.why: The queen on d8. The bishop is the only thing in the way, and it cannot stay there.

steps.text: So the bishop is stuck. A bishop can never stay on that column. The moment it moves, the queen is yours.

steps.ask: It has moved to b7. Collect the queen.
steps.hint: Straight up the d column now that nothing is in the way.
steps.wrongSay: Up the d column, all the way to d8.

steps.ask: What is the difference between an x-ray and a pin?

choices.text: A pin is an x-ray the front piece may not leave
Nothing, they are the same word

steps.why: Same line, same idea. In a pin the front piece cannot legally move. In an x-ray it can, but it dare not.

steps.text: Look through, not at.

lessons.name: Out of the Way
lessons.big: Empty a line, and do it with check.

steps.text: Sometimes your own piece is standing on the square you need. Move it out of the way, and do it with check.

steps.cap: The bishop wants the long diagonal. The knight is sitting on it.

steps.ask: Move the knight out of the way, with check, and give it away.
steps.hint: Nxf7 is check, and it leaves the diagonal open.
steps.wrongSay: It has to check them AND clear the diagonal. One square does both.

steps.text: They cannot take it. The king steps aside, and now the diagonal is open.

steps.ask: Now play the checkmate. Bring your queen to g7.
steps.hint: The queen takes on g7, and the bishop guards her from b2.
steps.wrongSay: Take on g7 with the queen.

steps.ask: Why does the clearing move have to be forcing?

choices.text: Otherwise they use the move to defend
It is a rule of chess

steps.why: Clearing a line costs a move. A check means they have no time to use theirs.

steps.text: Get out of the way, loudly.

lessons.name: Slam the Door
lessons.big: Put something between the guard and its job.

steps.text: Two of their pieces are talking to each other along a line. Stand something in the middle of it.

steps.cap: The rook on d8 is the only thing guarding the queen on d2. The line runs down the d column.

steps.ask: Block that line. Jump your knight to d6. It gives check at the same time.
steps.hint: Your knight can jump to d6. It is check, and it blocks the column.
steps.wrongSay: d6. It cuts the rook off from its queen.

steps.text: However they take the knight, the rook stops guarding for one move. That is enough.

steps.ask: They took with the c pawn. Now collect the queen.
steps.hint: Your queen takes theirs on d2.
steps.wrongSay: Take the queen on d2.

steps.text: Slam the door.

lessons.name: Treehouses and Highways
lessons.big: Where your pieces want to live.

steps.text: An outpost is a safe square on their side of the board. No pawn of theirs can ever reach it. A knight parked there can stay.

steps.ask: Tap the outpost this knight is standing on.
steps.hint: Which of their pawns could ever chase it off? None of them.
steps.why: No black pawn can get to c6 or e6, so nothing can chase the knight off d5. It is worth more than a bishop here.

steps.text: A column with no pawns on it is an open column. Rooks love those. The seventh row is the best place of all.

steps.ask: Take the seventh row with your rook.
steps.hint: Straight up the open d column to d7.
steps.wrongSay: The seventh row, where their pawns live.

steps.ask: Why is the seventh row so good for a rook?

choices.text: Their pawns are all on it, and their king is stuck behind
It is far away

steps.why: Everything on that row is a target. And their king cannot get close enough to chase it off.

steps.goal: Five endings. Where do the pieces want to be?

steps.text: Treehouses and highways.

lessons.name: Bones That Cannot Go Back
lessons.big: Pawns are the skeleton of the position.

steps.text: Pawns are the only pieces that cannot go back. Wherever you put them, they stay, and everything else has to live around them.

steps.ask: Tap the white pawn with no friendly pawn beside it.
steps.hint: Look at the c column and the e column next to it.
steps.why: An isolated pawn. No pawn can ever defend it, so a piece has to babysit it all game.

steps.text: That is the trade. A lonely pawn is weak. But the square just in front of it makes a lovely outpost.
Two bishops are worth more than you think. One covers the light squares. The other covers the dark ones.

steps.ask: Two bishops against two knights, in an open position. Who would you rather be?

choices.text: The bishops. They reach across the whole board
The knights

steps.why: With few pawns in the way the bishops rule. Block the position up with pawns and the knights come into their own.

steps.goal: Play a game. Notice which pawns you cannot take back, before you push them.

steps.text: Bones that cannot go back.

lessons.name: Your Openings as White
lessons.big: The same plan, every single game.

steps.text: You do not need twenty openings. You need one answer to each first move, played the same way every time.

steps.cap: Against 1...e5, the Italian. Bishop to c4, castle, rook to e1.

notes.7: 4. c3 — making room for d4 one day.
notes.13: 7. Re1 — this is the position you are aiming for.

steps.cap: Against 1...e6, take on d5 and play a simple game. Bishop d3, knight f3, castle.

notes.5: 3. exd5 — the Exchange French. Symmetrical and easy to play.
notes.9: 5. Bd3 — the same setup as always. That is the point of a repertoire.

steps.cap: Against 1...c6, the same idea. Take, then build the same little house.

notes.5: 3. exd5 — take, and the position looks like the French again.
notes.11: 6. Bf4 — bishop out before e3 shuts it in. The London move order.

steps.ask: Start the game. Push your king pawn two squares, to e4.
steps.hint: e4. One first move, every game.
steps.wrongSay: e4. Pick one and stick to it.

steps.ask: Why play the same opening every game?

choices.text: You reach positions you already understand
It saves work

steps.why: You are not learning moves by heart. You are collecting boards you have seen before.

steps.text: One answer to each first move.

lessons.name: Your Openings as Black
lessons.big: Copy the plan, and know the three traps.

steps.text: Black is easier. You need one answer to 1.e4 and one answer to 1.d4. That is all.

steps.cap: Against the Ruy Lopez: kick the bishop, develop, castle, play d6.

notes.6: 3... a6 — asking the bishop what it wants to do.
notes.14: 7... d6 — a solid house. Now the pieces come out behind it.

steps.cap: Against 1.d4: the Queen's Gambit Declined. Hold the centre with pawns.

notes.4: 2... e6 — declining the gambit, and opening the bishop.
notes.14: 7... c6 — solid as a brick. Nothing falls over here.

steps.text: And one trap to know. If they jump a knight to g5 attacking f7, do not panic.

steps.ask: Hit back in the middle. Push your d pawn two squares.
steps.hint: d5 attacks their bishop and opens your position.
steps.wrongSay: d5. Counter in the middle rather than defending f7.

steps.ask: They took on d5 and now attack your knight on c6. What now?

choices.text: Na5, hitting their bishop and getting out of the way
Give up the knight

steps.why: Na5 attacks the bishop on c4 and saves the knight. That is the whole defence.

steps.text: Copy the plan. Know the traps.

lessons.name: Key Squares
lessons.big: Get your king in front and the pawn queens.

steps.text: King and one pawn against a king is the ending everything else turns into. It is worth knowing exactly.

steps.cap: Your king is IN FRONT of the pawn and on the sixth row. This always wins.

steps.ask: Walk the king sideways to take the squares in front.
steps.hint: d6 or f6. Take the squares the pawn wants to walk through.
steps.wrongSay: Move the king, not the pawn. He goes first.

steps.text: Now the other version. Same pieces, but the king is BEHIND the pawn, and it is only a draw.

steps.ask: Aim your king at three squares on the sixth row. Tap all three.
steps.hint: Three squares in a row, two ranks ahead of the pawn.
steps.why: Get your king onto any of those and the pawn queens. They are the key squares.

steps.goal: Five endings. Count the moves rather than guessing.

steps.text: Get the king in front.

lessons.name: Bridges and Fences
lessons.big: The two rook endings everybody should know.

steps.text: Rook endings come up more than any other. Two positions cover most of them. Both have names.

steps.cap: The Lucena. Your pawn is nearly home; their rook keeps checking. Build a bridge.

steps.ask: Push their king away first. Check on the d column.
steps.hint: Rook to d1 is check, and the king has to leave.
steps.wrongSay: Give a check with the rook. d1.

steps.text: Then put the rook on the fourth row. Now it is a shield. Your king hides behind it.
The other one is the Philidor. If you are defending, keep your rook on the third row until their pawn comes.

steps.ask: Where does a rook belong when there is a passed pawn about?

choices.text: Behind it, whether it is yours or theirs
In front of it

steps.why: Behind your own pawn, it clears the way. Behind theirs, it gets more squares as that pawn moves up.

steps.text: A bridge and a fence.
To attack a castled king, bring more pieces than they have guarding it. Three against two is usually enough.

steps.cap: Bishop, knight and queen can all reach that corner. So the bishop rings the doorbell.

steps.ask: Give the bishop away on h7.
steps.hint: Bxh7 is check and drags the king out.
steps.wrongSay: h7. Give the bishop up on purpose.

steps.text: He takes. Then the knight arrives with check, and the queen follows it in.

steps.cap: The whole thing. Three pieces, and the king never gets away.

notes.3: 2. Ng5+ — the second attacker arrives with check.
notes.5: 3. Qh5 — and the third. Now there is no defence.
notes.15: 8. Qxg7# — checkmate, eight moves after the bishop went.

steps.ask: When should you NOT start an attack like this?

choices.text: When you have fewer attackers than they have defenders
Never, always attack

steps.why: Count first. An attack with two pieces against three defenders just loses the two pieces.

steps.text: Three beats two.

lessons.name: Name the Mate
lessons.big: You see it faster once it has a name.

steps.text: Checkmates come in shapes. Once a shape has a name you spot it far faster.

steps.cap: The smothered mate. His own rook and pawns do the work; the knight only has to arrive.

steps.ask: Play the checkmate. Jump your knight to f7 and the game is over.
steps.hint: The knight jumps to f7. Nothing can take it and he has nowhere to go.
steps.wrongSay: f7. Look at how boxed in he already is.

steps.text: The back row mate is another shape. So is the one where a rook and a bishop work together.

steps.ask: Why bother learning the names?

choices.text: You recognise the shape before you calculate anything
To sound clever

steps.why: Strong players do not work out more than you. They have seen more, so there is less to work out.

steps.goal: Five mates. See whether any of the shapes look familiar.

steps.text: Name it and you will see it.

lessons.name: A Plan Is a Sentence
lessons.big: I will do this, because of that.

steps.text: Tricks are not everything. There is one more question. Ask it every game: what am I trying to do here?
A plan is one sentence. I will do this, because of that. If you cannot say it, you do not have one.
Look at four things first. Is either king in danger. Who has more material. Whose pieces are doing more. Which pawns are weak.

steps.ask: You are a whole rook ahead. What is the plan?

choices.text: Trade pieces off. The fewer left, the bigger a rook is
Attack straight away

steps.why: Ahead on material, trade pieces and keep pawns. Behind, keep pieces on and complicate.

steps.ask: Their king is stuck in the middle and yours has castled. What is the plan?

choices.text: Open lines and go for him before he escapes
Wait and see

steps.why: A king in the middle is a temporary weakness. Use it now or it goes away.

steps.goal: Play a game and say your plan to yourself every five moves.

steps.text: I will do this, because of that.

lessons.name: Touch It, Move It
lessons.big: Clocks, notation, and how to behave.

steps.text: In a real match, a few rules change. None of them are hard.
Touch move. Make up your mind before you reach out. Touch a piece and you usually have to move it.
If a piece sits crooked, say "I adjust" out loud first. Then you may straighten it.

steps.ask: You pick up your knight, then see it loses a piece. What now?

choices.text: You have to move it if it has a legal move
Put it back and think again

steps.why: If that piece has a legal move you must play one. Decide before you reach out.

steps.text: Write your moves down as you play. Then offer a draw only after moving, before you press the clock.

steps.ask: Something has gone wrong and you need help. What do you do?

choices.text: Stop the clock and put your hand up
Call out to the room

steps.why: Stop both clocks, raise your hand and wait. The person who comes is the Tournament Director.

steps.text: And shake hands at the end, whoever won. That part matters more than the game did.
Touch it, move it. Write it down. Shake hands.
